1135.title: The seven mansions
1135.hook: Teresa's castle has seven dwelling places, and the King lives in the center
1135.carry: the king is in the center
1135.howItsDone: Carmelites and others who pray in Teresa's way read The Interior Castle slowly, often with a spiritual director, and speak of prayer as a journey inward toward God dwelling at the center of the soul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four ways to water a garden: buckets, a wheel, a stream, and rain. Your line was sometimes buckets, sometimes rain.

Later, Teresa is asked to write again, this time for her sisters. She says she didn't know how to begin. Then a new picture came to her: the soul as a castle, made of a single diamond or very clear crystal, with many rooms, some above, some below, some to the sides. In the very center is the main room, where the most secret things pass between God and the soul. The King lives there. Plenty of souls, she says, stay out in the courtyard, around the outer wall, with no idea what's inside their own house. The book is The Interior Castle; you first stepped inside on day two hundred seventy-six.
screen: `MANY ROOMS, AND ONE AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Teresa groups the rooms into seven dwelling places, and she took the word from Jesus. In John's Gospel he says, "In my Father's house are many mansions." In the King James English, mansion means a dwelling place, a room to stay in, not a big house on a hill. Teresa's Spanish word is moradas, dwellings. So the seven mansions aren't seven buildings. They're seven depths of one soul, the way rooms go further into a house. The door of this castle, she says, is prayer and reflection: not cleverness or technique, just turning toward God honestly and paying attention. The outer rooms are crowded. She says snakes and vermin from outside creep in with you there: distractions, worries, the business of the day. That's no reason to stay out; it's just what the first rooms are like. Further in, it gets quieter, and the light from the center reaches further. Prayer becomes less something you do and more something that happens to you, like yesterday's rain. In her picture, the King isn't far away. He's in the center of the soul, already. The castle is beautiful because he's in it, she says, and nothing we do can take that beauty away, though sin can cover it, like a black cloth thrown over a crystal in the sun. The light is still shining underneath. For Teresa, the journey inward isn't a hunt for a missing God. It's coming home to the room where, she says, he has been the whole time.
screen: `IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE ARE MANY MANSIONS.`
`THE KING IS ALREADY AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Notice where you are in Teresa's picture, out in the noisy courtyard or a first room where worries crawl in too, and don't fight it. Take one step further: one more breath of attention, one layer quieter. If you pray, turn toward the King at the center without needing to reach him; if you don't, just notice that there's an inside, and rest there.
The seven mansions. Teresa's dwelling places of the soul, one inside another, opening toward the center, where the King lives.
Your line: the king is in the center. The light still shines under the cloth. Until tomorrow.

1136.title: Nada
1136.hook: John of the Cross: nothing, nothing, nothing, and on the mountain, nothing: letting go for love
1136.howItsDone: Carmelites and others who follow John of the Cross practice detachment, letting go of attachments to things, comforts and even spiritual feelings, so that the heart is free to love God; it is often taught with a spiritual director.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's castle of clear crystal, room inside room. Your line was the king is in the center.

A small sketch of a mountain, drawn by hand. At the bottom, paths split off. On the wrong roads, the drawing is labeled with the things people chase: having, knowing, comfort, glory. Up the narrow middle path, one word repeats, again and again, and near the top of the mountain, the same word once more. Nada. Nothing. The sketch was made by a Spanish Carmelite friar, Teresa's companion in reforming their order, known as John of the Cross; you met his dark night on day two hundred seventy-seven. And nada sounds, at first, like a bleak word to put on a mountain.

Here's what John means, and it isn't despair. In The Ascent of Mount Carmel, he gives short sayings that work like a riddle. To come to enjoy everything, desire to enjoy nothing. To come to possess everything, desire to possess nothing. To come to know everything, desire to know nothing. Nada is the price, and todo, everything, is the prize. The nothing is for the sake of the all. Why? A heart full of grasping has no room left. If your hands are clenched around a pile of small things, you can't receive the one great thing. So the nothing isn't hatred of the world. Mountains, rivers, the night air: John's poems are full of them. The nothing is about the grip, letting go of the clutch, the need to own, so that love has space. Paul says something close in his letter to the Philippians: "I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord." Not that everything is worthless; next to the one thing, he can let the rest go. John isn't gentle about how hard this is. Letting go can feel like loss, like night. Yet his mountain is drawn going up. The narrow path of nothing is the one that reaches the top, and near the summit, where the word is nada again, he places God's honor and glory. In John's picture, empty hands at the top turn out to be full.
screen: `NADA IS THE PRICE, TODO THE PRIZE.`
`NOT HATRED OF THE WORLD, LOOSER GRIP.`

segments.voice: Close one hand into a firm fist, feel the grip, and ask what you're gripping right now: an object, a plan, being right in an argument, an image of yourself. Pick just one, and slowly, a finger at a time, not in disgust, let the fist uncurl and your hold on that one thing loosen with it. If you pray, offer it to God as the hand opens; if you don't, just feel the difference between the grip and the release.
Nada. Spanish for nothing. In John of the Cross, the letting go that makes room for everything, for love.
Your line: nothing, for all. A clenched hand can't receive. Rest well.

1137.title: The living flame
1137.hook: John's poem of love like a flame that wounds gently
1137.howItsDone: Carmelites and other readers of John of the Cross pray with his poems slowly, sometimes aloud, and his Living Flame of Love is read in retreats on the work of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nada: John of the Cross and the narrow path of nothing up the mountain. Your line was nothing, for all.

Same friar, a different voice. Yesterday John of the Cross was drawing a steep mountain with nothing written up its side. Today he's writing a love poem. It opens with a cry, which in English runs something like this: O living flame of love, that tenderly wounds my soul in its deepest center. Wounds, and tenderly, in the same breath. That's not how burns usually go. The man who taught letting go of everything also wrote lines this warm, and wrote them about God. For John, the two belong together.

John wrote the poem, and then, because a friend asked, a long commentary explaining it line by line. The flame, he says, is the Holy Spirit, an old image in the Bible. At Pentecost, the book of Acts says, "there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." And the Song of Songs says love's coals "are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame." So why would a loving flame wound? John uses a picture from the hearth. Put a damp log on a fire. At first the fire doesn't look friendly. The log hisses, blackens, smokes, and lets out the water it was holding. That's the hard part, the purifying. But the fire is the same fire the whole time. It isn't angry at the log. It's turning the log into itself. In the end the wood glows, and you can't tell where the log stops and the flame begins. For John, that's what God's love does to a person. The pain of being changed and the joy of being loved are one fire, felt at different stages. So the wound is tender: love that hurts only because it's getting in. And notice where the flame reaches: the deepest center, the same center Teresa put the King in, two days ago. The two friends seem to point at the same room. One built a castle around it. The other set it on fire.
screen: `ONE FIRE: THE HURT AND THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: If you can do it safely, light a candle and just watch; if you can't, call a flame to mind, or look at a picture of one. See how it moves, where it's blue and where it's gold, and how it turns whatever it touches into more of itself. If you pray, let it stand for the Holy Spirit, as John did; if you don't, just watch the light, and blow out any real flame before the end.
The living flame. John of the Cross's image of the Holy Spirit's love: a fire that wounds gently, burns away what's damp, and turns the soul into flame.
Your line: o living flame. In John's poem, love reaches the deepest center. See you tomorrow.

1138.title: Pots and pans
1138.hook: Brother Lawrence, a Carmelite cook, turning an omelette for the love of God
1138.howItsDone: Christians across churches read Brother Lawrence's The Practice of the Presence of God and try to keep a simple awareness of God through ordinary work, turning back to God briefly and often during the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the living flame: a damp log turned to glow. Your line was o living flame.

A monastery kitchen in Paris. Steam, noise, people calling for things all at once. At the stove stands a lay brother of the Carmelites, a former soldier, by his own account clumsy, who says he had a great dislike for kitchen work. His name in religion is Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection, and you first met him at this stove on day two hundred seventy-eight. He left no big book: some letters, and a visiting priest's notes of their conversations, published after his death and known in English by a title that stuck, The Practice of the Presence of God.
screen: `THE PRACTICE OF THE PRESENCE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Lawrence's secret, as he told it, was almost embarrassingly simple. He would turn the little cake frying in the pan for the love of God. When it was done, if there was nothing else to do, he'd bow down and thank God, and then get up again, happier than a king. He'd pick a piece of straw off the ground, for the love of God. The task didn't matter; what mattered was who he did it for. He said that for him the time of work didn't differ from the time of prayer. In the noise and clatter of his kitchen, with several people calling for different things, he said he had God as calmly as if he were on his knees before the sacrament. That's the whole teaching: not a technique, but a habit of turning toward God in the middle of things, and turning back whenever you notice you've wandered off. He wasn't hard on himself about the wandering. When he forgot, he admitted it, and came back. Paul had said it long before: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." And again: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." Lawrence just took Paul at his word, in a kitchen. Two days ago it was John's mountain of nothing; yesterday, his flame. Lawrence belongs to the same family, and he brings it down to the stove. The holy place, for him, was wherever his hands were.
screen: `TURN THE CAKE FOR THE LOVE OF GOD.`
`WHATSOEVER YE DO, AS TO THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Think of the next ordinary thing your hands will do, making coffee, a sandwich, folding a towel, washing a pan, and picture doing it slowly, all the way through. Then decide who it's for: if you pray, the love of God, the way Lawrence turned his cake; if you don't, someone you love, or simply full attention. Let the plain task be enough.
Pots and pans. Brother Lawrence's kitchen, where turning a cake for the love of God was as much prayer as kneeling in church.
Your line: turn it for love. Wandering off and coming back is part of it. I'll be here tomorrow.

1139.title: Principle and foundation
1139.hook: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God; use things as far as they help
1139.howItsDone: Jesuits and others who make the Spiritual Exercises, in a long retreat or in daily life with a guide, usually begin by praying with the Principle and Foundation, and return to it when making decisions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pots and pans: Brother Lawrence turning the cake for the love of God. Your line was turn it for love.

A Basque soldier is carried home with a shattered leg. Stuck in bed for a long recovery, he asks for adventure stories. The house doesn't have any. What it has is a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives. He reads them, out of boredom, and something in him turns. That's how his own Autobiography tells it. His name is Ignatius of Loyola, and you first met him on day eight hundred seventy-three. Out of what happened next came a small handbook for a guide leading someone through prayer: the Spiritual Exercises. A new room today, the Ignatian way, and it starts with one short paragraph the whole handbook stands on.

Here's the paragraph, in plain words. Human beings are created to praise, reverence and serve God our Lord, and so to save their souls. Everything else on the face of the earth is created for us, to help us toward that end. So we should use things as far as they help us toward it, and let go of them as far as they get in the way. It sounds dry, almost like an engineer wrote it. But it doesn't sort the world into holy things and bad things. Money, a job, a phone, a friendship, an ambition: none of it is the enemy, and none of it is the point. Each one gets the same quiet question: does it help? The measure is the purpose, not the thing. Paul had asked a similar question about Christian freedom: "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient." His Greek word for expedient, sympherei, means it's useful, it helps. Plenty is allowed; not all of it helps. And the opening line matters as much as the rule. Ignatius starts with what we're for: praise, reverence, service. Revelation gives that note to the elders around God's throne: "Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things." Begin there, in Ignatius's way of seeing, and every choice gets simpler, if not always easier: not what do I want, but what helps?
screen: `USE THINGS AS FAR AS THEY HELP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that takes up real space in your life, an app, a habit, a possession, and without judging it yet, hold it up and ask: does this help me toward what I'm for? If you pray, you can ask God to show you; if you don't, ask whether it helps you love and serve well. Notice the answer, even if it's mixed.
Principle and foundation. The opening of Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises: we're made to praise, reverence and serve God, and we use everything else as far as it helps.
Your line: as far as it helps. Not good or bad, just: does it help? Until tomorrow.

1140.title: Indifference
1140.hook: not coldness but freedom: not preferring health to sickness, wealth to poverty, for their own sake
1140.howItsDone: In Ignatian spirituality, people making a decision pray first for indifference, the inner freedom to choose whatever best serves God, often with a spiritual director, before weighing the options.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the principle and foundation: use everything as far as it helps. Your line was as far as it helps.

Call someone indifferent today and it's an insult. It means they don't care: the shrug, the blank text back, the person who walks past. So it's a jolt to find the word in Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises as something to want. In the same paragraph as yesterday's foundation, he says we need to make ourselves indifferent to all created things. Not wanting health more than sickness, riches more than poverty, honor more than dishonor, a long life more than a short one. Taken one way, that sounds cold, even inhuman. Ignatius means nearly the opposite.

None of these things is wanted for its own sake, and Ignatius limits it to what is left to our free choice and not forbidden. He isn't saying sickness is as good as health, or that nobody should look after a body or pay the rent. He's saying don't let any one of those things own you. If you need to be healthy, rich and admired no matter what, those needs make your choices for you. You aren't free. Indifference, for Ignatius, is balance: standing like a scale that hasn't tipped yet, so the only weight that tips it is what God is asking, what serves love. Then comes the second half of his sentence, which is all desire: we should want and choose only what helps us toward the end we're made for. So indifference isn't wanting nothing. It's wanting one thing so much that everything else can move. Paul writes from prison, to the Philippians: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound." Learned, notice. Not born with it. And a Gospel scene has the same shape: Jesus in the garden the night before he dies. He doesn't pretend he wants the cross. He asks for the cup to pass. And then: "nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." That's not coldness. It's freedom, and a warm kind: a real preference, said out loud, and then held open.
screen: `NOT AS I WILL, BUT AS THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: Choose something you're hoping for right now, a result, a reply, a plan, and let yourself want it honestly; then picture both outcomes and see whether love could still be found in the other one. If you pray, say the line from the garden, not as I will, but as thou wilt, meaning only as much as you can; if not, let the hope sit beside the other outcome, both in view.
Indifference. In Ignatius, not coldness but freedom: wanting nothing created for its own sake, so you're free to choose what serves God and love.
Your line: free to choose love. Wanting one thing lets everything else move. Go gently.

He means feelings get in the way, so a good Christian stops wanting anything.
He means hiding your wishes, even in prayer, so that God won't see them.
chat.meaning: Ignatian indifference is balance, a scale not yet tipped. It isn't coldness or wanting nothing, but freedom to choose what serves God and love.

1141.title: The first week: loved sinner
1141.hook: the Exercises begin with honest sorrow held by mercy
1141.howItsDone: In the Spiritual Exercises, whether in a long silent retreat or in daily life with a guide, the first week is spent praying over sin and God's mercy, often ending in a conversation with Christ on the cross and, for Catholics, sometimes in confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatian indifference: not coldness, but a preference held open. Your line was free to choose love.

Ignatius divides his Spiritual Exercises into weeks. A week, in his book, isn't seven days. He says plainly that some people will take longer over a week and some shorter, depending on what they're given. A week is a stage, a movement of the heart, and the first is the hard one. Ignatius asks the person praying to look honestly at sin: the angels' sin, Adam and Eve's, and then their own. That sounds grim. But the way he sets it up, the looking never happens alone.

Ignatius doesn't ask anyone to stare at their failures in an empty room. He asks them to do it standing before Christ on the cross, and to talk with him the way one friend talks to another, asking three plain questions. What have I done for Christ? What am I doing for Christ? What ought I to do for Christ? That's the frame of the whole week. The sorrow is real; Ignatius even asks for the grace of tears. But it's sorrow in front of one who, Christians say, already died for the one praying. Paul puts it this way: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." While we were yet sinners. Not after we cleaned up. Somewhere in the first week, Ignatius has the person praying break into wonder. Why didn't the earth swallow me? Why have the sun and the stars, the fruits and the animals, the angels and the saints, all gone on holding me up? In Ignatius's telling, the answer is mercy, there the whole time. Jesus's story of the son who comes home has the picture: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." The father runs before the son can say a word of his speech. That's the first week: a loved sinner, both words true at once. Look back over this week of going inward, from Teresa's castle to Ignatius's freedom, and it ends here: in his picture, the one who comes home finds the door already open.
screen: `WHAT HAVE I DONE, AM DOING, OUGHT I TO DO?`

segments.voice: Let one thing you've done wrong come to mind, something real but not the heaviest thing you carry; this is two minutes, not a lifetime. Name it plainly, without excuses and without piling on, and imagine it held, not thrown back at you. If you pray, bring it before Christ on the cross and ask Ignatius's three questions; if you don't, hold it next to the picture of a father running down a road.
The first week. The opening stage of Ignatius's Exercises: honest sorrow for sin, held in front of a mercy that came first.
Your line: loved, as I am. Honest sorrow and mercy, held together at once. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Isn't looking hard at your sins just a recipe for feeling terrible about yourself?
options: No. Ignatius has you look before Christ on the cross, as a loved sinner held by mercy.
It's meant to; the worse you feel, the more God will forgive you in the end.
Not really, because the first week skips sin and looks only at what's good in you.
chat.meaning: In Ignatius's first week the looking never happens alone: it's sorrow before Christ on the cross, with mercy there the whole time. A loved sinner, both true.
